Document Analysis & Organizational Synthesis
From Scattered Papers to an Energy-Smart Scheduling Strategy
Five linked reports analysing the 31-paper Document Set on steelmaking and furnace scheduling: DRL, digital twins, XAI and metallurgical constraints.
The story in five acts
Task 1
Inventory & Initial Scan
Metadata for all 31 papers, the boundaries of the domain, the toolbox, and how reliable automated extraction turned out to be.
Task 2
Topic Tree & Cross-Reference Network
4 clusters, 11 sub-topics, a network graph and a co-occurrence matrix showing where knowledge is concentrated and where it is missing.
Task 3
Synthesis Divergence
Six tensions between approaches, a trade-off matrix and how mature the evidence is.
Task 4
Integrative Blueprint
Explainable Twin-in-the-Loop Scheduling: architecture, decision rights, organisation, roadmap, KPIs and risks.
Task 5
Executive Briefing (AIDA)
Attention → Interest → Desire → Action, ending in a concrete 90-day ask.
Key findings at a glance
31
papers, 2016–2026, 456 pages. 22 are about steel or metal processes
4
citation links inside the set: fragmented knowledge
0
papers combining energy scheduling with XAI, or DRL + DT + XAI
5.8–13%
energy-cost reductions reported in the set (not a site forecast)
Scheduling methods proven in steel plants are rigid and hard to explain. Adaptive methods (DRL) have only been tested in simulation and are black boxes. Explaining decisions has been demonstrated only outside steel. The blueprint integrates all three behind metallurgical guardrails and human decision rights.

Method note: reports were produced with AI assistance (text extraction, coding and drafting). Every figure quoted was checked against the source PDFs. Cluster tags and trade-off ratings are analytical judgements and are labelled as such.

Inventory & Initial Scan of the Document Set
31 papers left behind by a departed engineer: what they are, who wrote them, and where the knowledge domain begins and ends.

1. What the scan tells us
The main finding:
the archive is not a random pile. It is a recent (mostly 2020–2026) and applied collection built around one question:
how do we schedule energy-hungry steel processes when conditions keep changing?
But it has
no index, no summary and almost no links between papers
. Only 4 of the 31 papers cite another paper in the set (see Task 2). The engineer's knowledge was in their head, not in the archive.
Core (cluster A, 16 papers):
scheduling of furnaces, rolling, casting and heat-treatment lines, mostly with operations-research methods and metaheuristics. Across the whole set, 22 papers deal with steel or metal processes and 17 have an explicit energy objective.
New layer (clusters B–D, 15 papers):
deep reinforcement learning (6 papers), digital twins (5), explainable AI (6) and human-centric AI (7); the counts overlap. Most are from 2022 or later, and none of the DRL papers was deployed live in a steel plant.
Geography:
China dominates (16 papers), with Germany second (5). European papers are the ones that carry the human-centric and XAI thinking (

,

).

4. Extraction method & data quality
Metadata was extracted in two passes.
Pass 1 (automated):
extract_metadata.py
(in the ZIP) uses
pdfinfo
and
pdftotext
plus regular expressions to pull the embedded title and author, DOI, keyword block, year and abstract snippet.
Pass 2 (human check):
every field was checked against the first page of each PDF and corrected. The automated pass alone was not reliable enough to use:
Field (automated pass)
Usable
Why it failed
Title in embedded PDF metadata
21/31
Publisher PDFs often ship with an empty or generic
Title
field → titles were read from page 1.
Author in embedded PDF metadata
15/31
Least reliable field; several PDFs duplicate or garble author blocks (e.g.
D11
repeats each name 3–4×).
Keyword block found by regex
30/31
D15
has no keyword list; keywords were inferred from its abstract and flagged.
Publication year guessed correctly
20/31
Most-frequent year on page 1 picks up received/online dates or cited years (e.g. online 2017 vs issue 2019 for
D02
).
Lesson for the organisation: automation speeds up the scan, but a human still has to validate the output. The same principle comes back in Tasks 4–5.

energy, furnace, DRL, uncertainty, XAI
; full list in
data/network_edges.csv
). Two papers are linked when their tags overlap enough (Jaccard similarity ≥ 0.34). Real citations between papers were added on top, after checking them in each reference list, along with one link for a shared research group. Node size = degree. Communities were detected with the Louvain method.

Diverging Approaches & the Trade-offs We Cannot Avoid
A deep contrast of the key sub-topics from Task 2: where the papers disagree, why, and what that forces the organisation to decide.
Task 2 identified the sub-topics where the archive is dense (furnace and rolling scheduling) and the isolated ones the organisation wants to adopt (DRL, digital twins, XAI). This report puts them side by side on purpose. The goal is not to pick a winner but to surface the
unavoidable trade-offs
any strategy has to take a position on.
6
tensions, each backed by at least 3 papers on each side

The six tensions
Tension 1
Guaranteed optimality vs. real-time adaptivity
Sub-topics A1/A2/A5 vs B2 · Should the scheduler be a mathematical model or a learned policy?
Exact & provable methods
D23
: online reheat-furnace algorithms with
proven best-possible competitive ratios
, but only for a single furnace with no breakdowns.
D01
: polynomial-time optimum for idle energy when the energy function is concave.
D28
: Benders decomposition solves the hot strip mill model
exactly only for small instances
; large ones need MOPSO.
D31
: the MILP reaches optimality only on small instances; a GA wins on large ones.
Strength: auditable, constraint-safe, and explainable by construction (you can read the model).
Deep reinforcement learning
D05
: SAC-based energy framework is
~100× faster than a commercial solver
and costs less than half of manual operation.
D09
: EAF-plant policy with minimal online compute that stays robust to mis-specified uncertainty, but has a
5.75% optimality gap vs MILP
in the deterministic case (6.5% on a larger instance).
D30
: DQN agent handles stochastic job arrivals without retraining, but
initial training took ≈10.7 h
for 4 jobs (≈14 min to retrain).
D20
,
D21
: reward design and convergence time are the weak points; LLM-written rewards are sometimes invalid.
Trade-off:
exact methods give certainty but become slow as the plant scales and changes; DRL gives speed under uncertainty but costs a few percent of optimality, needs heavy training, and offers no guarantee.
What it means for us:
neither side wins outright. Use exact or matheuristic planning where time allows (day-ahead), and learned policies where it doesn't (intra-day reaction). The DRL policy should be benchmarked against the MILP, as D09 does.
Tension 2
Physics fidelity vs. data-driven speed
Sub-topics A1/A4/C1 · How should furnace energy be modelled: thermodynamics or machine learning?
Physics-based / hybrid simulation
D01
: on/off/stand-by mode graphs
under-estimate achievable savings
; the full thermal dynamics must be modelled.
D27
: hybrid thermodynamic simulation inside the optimiser gives ~10% global / ~6% energy improvement, but
modelling and data effort is the main adoption barrier
.
D05
,
D24
: gas transmission, steam heat conduction and gas-holder mass balances are built in as hard physics constraints.
Pure data-driven models
D14
: GA-BP network predicts furnace energy per ton with 94.7% accuracy, yet the authors themselves call for
physics + data hybrids to gain interpretability and generalisability
.
D19
: LightGBM rolling-force model (MAPE 0.56%) only works once HSR and CSR data silos are merged into one "data continent".
D10
: the digital twin tracks timing within 0.98% but
ignores slab temperature
, the metallurgically critical variable.
Trade-off:
physics models transfer to new conditions and can be explained, but they are expensive to build; data models are cheap and accurate inside their training range, but opaque and brittle outside it.
What it means for us:
the digital twin at the heart of the blueprint should be hybrid: physics for heat transfer and hard constraints, ML for the parameters that drift. A pure black-box energy predictor would be neither trusted nor safe.
Tension 3
Robust (plan for the worst) vs. reactive (fix it when it happens)
Sub-topics A2/A3/B1 · How do we handle breakdowns, late heats and fluctuating prices?
Proactive / robust scheduling
D28
: robust optimisation over the worst-case rolling times.
D02
: pre-compressed processing times absorb breakdowns; robustness
and
stability as twin objectives.
D07
: fuzzy gas heating values, processing times and due dates.
Risk:
conservatism
. Buffers waste furnace time, and furnace time is energy.
Reactive / dynamic rescheduling
D18
: three disturbance levels → fine-tune, local machine swap, or global reschedule.
D03
: forecast release times, then chance-constrained rescheduling online.
D24
: rolling horizon; a
shorter horizon means less gas flaring but more compute
, and forecast error dominates.
D23
: online algorithms decide without knowing future orders.
Risk:
schedule nervousness
. Operators lose confidence if the plan changes constantly.
Trade-off:
robustness costs efficiency up front; reactivity costs stability and operator trust.
What it means for us:
adopt D18's tiered logic as the organisational rule. Absorb small disturbances locally, escalate large ones, and make every escalation visible and explained to operators (the link to Tension 5).
Tension 4
Local optimisation vs. plant-wide integration
Sub-topics A1 vs A3/B1 · Optimise one furnace, or the whole hot chain?
Single unit / single stage
D15
: grey-wolf furnace charging saves 12–30 min per furnace
with no capital investment
. A quick win.
D23
: a single reheating furnace.
D14
: prediction for one furnace type.
Tractable and fast to deploy, but savings at one stage can create waiting (and heat loss) at the next.
Integrated multi-stage
D17
: furnace + rolling solved jointly beats single-stage models; the authors want to add gas and energy media next.
D12
: SCC + ladle dispatching:
−1.21% energy at constant productivity
. Modest, but plant-wide and free.
D19
: breaking HSR/CSR data silos raised thickness and flatness hit rates.
D28
: rolling start times are optimised
because
they drive reheating heat loss.
Trade-off:
integration captures the coupling (hot charging, ladle heat, gas balance) but multiplies model size, data needs and organisational coordination.
What it means for us:
start locally for credibility, but design interfaces for integration from day one. The furnace–rolling boundary is where the set shows the largest coupled energy effect.
Tension 5
Autonomy vs. human agency
Sub-topics B2 vs D1/D2/C2 · Who decides: the algorithm or the operator?
Autonomous optimisation
Most of cluster A and all DRL papers assume the schedule is executed as computed. Humans appear only as a manual-planning baseline to beat (
D15
,
D22
,
D27
).
D09
,
D05
: the value of DRL is precisely that decisions come too fast for a human to review each one.
Risk: black-box decisions in a high-temperature, high-consequence plant.
Explainable, human-in/on-the-loop
D25
: argues for
intelligence augmentation
. Human-on-the-loop for routine control, human-in-the-loop for high-consequence decisions; AI–human conflict is itself a risk.
D13
: SHAP explanations of a multi-agent PPO controller, designed per user role (+22% reward vs FIFO).
D08
: counterfactuals ("what would have to change for a better outcome").
D04
: decision trees that make GA schedules understandable to shop-floor staff.
D11
,
D16
: operators can override or approve plans.
D06
: EU ALTAI trustworthiness criteria.
Trade-off:
full autonomy maximises speed; human oversight adds latency but provides accountability, catches model errors, and determines whether the system gets used at all.
What it means for us:
the XAI evidence is from generic job shops. No paper explains energy-scheduling decisions in steel (Task 2 finding). We must transfer the XAI techniques, not wait for the literature.
Tension 6
Energy
consumption
vs. energy
cost
vs. delivery
Sub-topics A4 vs B2 · What exactly are we minimising?
Minimise GJ / kWh (plus tardiness)
D07
: gas energy vs weighted tardiness is a real Pareto trade-off.
D22
: up to −13% energy cost and −90% tardiness on a steel heat-treatment line (the best-reported joint gain).
D14
,
D15
,
D29
,
D31
: physical energy or idle time.
Minimise € under time-varying prices
D09
: EAF plant scheduled against electricity spot prices and on-site renewables; optimises cost, not kWh.
D21
: demand-response MAPPO −5.8% cost vs single-agent PPO by shifting load to cheap hours.
D27
: demonstrates shifting furnace demand to follow flexible prices.
Trade-off:
load shifting can
lower cost while raising consumption
(e.g. holding furnaces hot to wait for a price dip), and energy gains can come at the expense of delivery.
What it means for us:
the organisation must set the objective hierarchy explicitly (safety/metallurgy → delivery → € → GJ/CO₂). Otherwise each algorithm will quietly optimise something different.

The central tension, in one sentence:
the methods that are
proven in steel plants
(metaheuristics, dynamic rule-based scheduling, agent systems, one IoT twin) are rigid and hard to explain to operators, while the methods that are
adaptive and fast
(DRL) have only been tested in simulation and are black boxes. Explaining
decisions
, which is what would make the adaptive methods acceptable, has been demonstrated only outside steel. The organisation cannot adopt any one cluster as it stands; it has to
integrate
them (Task 4).
Mandatory decisions the organisation faces
Planning architecture:
which decisions stay with exact or matheuristic planning, and which move to learned real-time policies?
Model investment:
how much do we invest in physics-based twin models versus faster data-driven shortcuts?
Disturbance policy:
how much buffer do we accept, and what size of disturbance triggers a global reschedule?
Scope:
which stage do we start with, and when do we integrate furnace, rolling and the energy network?
Autonomy level:
which decisions can run with a human on the loop, and which need a human in the loop?
Objective hierarchy:
when metallurgy, delivery, € and GJ conflict, which one wins?

The Unified Organisational Blueprint
Re-converging DRL, digital twins and XAI with established metallurgical constraints into one implementable strategy.
The blueprint in one line:
an
Explainable Twin-in-the-Loop Scheduling
system. Metallurgical guardrails bound a hybrid digital twin; a mathematical planner sets the daily envelope; a DRL agent trained in the twin reacts in real time inside that envelope; and every decision reaches operators with an explanation in energy and metallurgical terms, under decision rights that widen only as trust is earned.
1. Design principles: how each Task 3 tension is resolved
Principle 1 · Resolves Tension 1 & 6
Hard metallurgy first, optimisation second
Metallurgical rules are coded as
guardrails
(constraints and action masks) that no optimiser or agent can override. D09 already restricts the DRL action space to domain-knowledge rules; D05 and D24 embed physics constraints.
Principle 2 · Resolves Tension 1 & 3
Plan with math, react with learning
A matheuristic or robust day-ahead plan (D22, D28, D17) sets the envelope. Inside it, a DRL agent (D09, D05) handles intra-day disturbances and price moves. Provable online rules (D23) are the fallback if the agent is unavailable or out of distribution.
Principle 3 · Resolves Tension 2 & 4
One hybrid twin as the single source of truth
Physics for heat (D01, D27), ML for drifting parameters (D14, D19), and logistics timing (D10) on one plant data layer that removes silos (D19). The DRL agent is trained
only
in the twin, never on the live plant (D30).
Principle 4 · Resolves Tension 3
Tiered disturbance response
Small → local fine-tuning; medium → machine swap; large → global reschedule with human approval (D18). This limits schedule nervousness.
Principle 5 · Resolves Tension 5 (the Task 2 gap)
Every decision explainable in energy and metallurgical terms
Apply SHAP (D13), counterfactuals (D08) and tree surrogates (D04) to energy scheduling: “this slab waits 6 min because charging it now would cost X GJ and violate Y”.
Principle 6 · Resolves Tension 5
Autonomy is earned, not assumed
Autonomy is granted per decision class and is reversible: human-in-the-loop → human-on-the-loop only after gates are met (D25). Operator override is always available and logged (D11, D16).

Why a cell, not a project
The archive shows what happens when knowledge sits with one person: 31 papers, 4 cross-citations, no synthesis. The cell makes knowledge institutional. Guardrails, models, rewards and explanations are versioned artefacts with named owners, and every automated decision leaves a trace.

Executive Briefing: Scheduling Our Way to Lower Energy Costs
From 31 scattered papers to one decision: an explainable, twin-trained, human-governed scheduling programme for the furnace and rolling chain.
Executive summary · decision requested
Approve a 90-day foundation phase
for an
Explainable Twin-in-the-Loop Scheduling
programme on the reheating-furnace and hot-rolling chain. Studies in the archive we inherited report
5.8–13% lower energy cost
from smarter scheduling in other plants. Our advantage is to combine what no single study has combined: learning-based speed, digital-twin fidelity, and decisions operators can understand and override.

I · Interest
DRL + digital twins make adaptive scheduling possible
D · Desire
XAI makes it safe and trusted
A · Action
A gated 36-month plan, starting in 90 days

Why now:
the archive already contains the building blocks. They are just not connected. Every phase ends at a gate where it either proves its value or stops. The only choice that can't be undone is to keep scheduling without energy in the picture while prices and carbon constraints tighten.
